lead: A gyroscope is a spinning mass. Once spinning, its axis stays pointed in the same direction in inertial space unless a torque acts on it. Push the axis and it does not move the way you pushed; it moves at right angles, a motion called precession. Aircraft use this to sense attitude, heading and turn rate without looking outside. This chapter gives the angular momentum law behind rigidity, calculates precession from torque, explains the short wobble called nutation, lists the drift errors that remain, and names the three cockpit gyro instruments.
prereq: You need: torque, moment of inertia and angular velocity from basic rotational mechanics; the navigation frame is introduced in 5.1, and the autopilot that consumes gyro signals is in Unit 1, Flight Control Systems.

sections.h3: Rigidity in space and the gimbal

blocks.text: A rotor spinning about its axis carries angular momentum. The size is H = Iω. I is the moment of inertia in kg·m², ω is the spin rate in rad/s, and H is in kg·m²/s. With no external torque, H stays fixed in inertial space. That is rigidity in space: the spin axis keeps its direction while the aircraft turns around it.

blocks.where: H is angular momentum in kg·m²/s; I is moment of inertia in kg·m²; ω is spin rate in rad/s.

blocks.text: A free gyro has three degrees of freedom: spin about its own axis, and tilt about two perpendicular gimbal axes. A cockpit instrument uses two of these as its measurement axes and lets the third carry the spin. Two degrees of freedom are enough to report pitch and roll, or heading and bank, while the case moves with the aircraft.

Gimbals can line up. When two axes become parallel, one degree of freedom is lost and the gyro cannot respond in that direction. This is gimbal lock. Caging locks the rotor during violent manoeuvres or before start. Erection is the slow levelling of the gyro to the local vertical, done with pendulous vanes or small torque motors.

A torque changes angular momentum: T = dH/dt. T is torque in N·m, H is angular momentum in kg·m²/s, and t is time in s. The change dH points along T. The tip of the H arrow moves toward T, so the spin axis swings at right angles to the push, not along it.
T = dH/dt    and    Ω = T/H = T/(Iω)
blocks.where: T is torque in N·m; H is angular momentum in kg·m²/s; t is time in s; Ω is steady precession rate in rad/s; I is moment of inertia in kg·m²; ω is spin rate in rad/s.

blocks.text: For a steady torque, the axis precesses at Ω = T/H. A large I or a fast spin gives a large H and a small Ω, so the axis resists the push. A rotor at 24,000 rpm is stiff for this reason. Direction follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers from H toward T, and the thumb gives the precession direction in the sense of the spin.

Apply a torque suddenly and the axis overshoots before settling into steady precession. The short wobble is nutation. Some syllabi call nutation the wobble and precession the topple. Damping, such as viscous fluid or eddy currents, removes nutation; without damping it would ring for a long time.

Real drift comes from bearing friction, rotor imbalance and case motion. Apparent drift comes from the Earth turning under the gyro. About the local vertical, the rate is 15.04 × sin(φ) °/h, where φ is latitude. It is 15.04 °/h at the poles and zero at the equator. Flying east or west adds a transport rate because the aircraft changes longitude over the curved Earth.

blocks.where: Ω<sub>app</sub> is apparent drift about the local vertical in degrees per hour; φ is latitude in degrees; 15.04 °/h is Earth's rotation rate.

blocks.text: Ring laser gyros and fibre-optic gyros replace the spinning mass with light travelling in a closed path. They have no bearings to wear and no warm-up spin. Their internal detail is in 5.5.

figure.caption: The rotor's angular momentum H = 50.3 kg·m²/s is tilted by a 0.01 N·m torque; the axis then precesses at 0.68 °/min. Notice that precession is at right angles to the torque, and nutation appears only when the torque is applied suddenly.

spec.title: Torque, momentum and precession
spec.aria: A cycle in which a spinning rotor carries angular momentum, an applied torque tilts that momentum vector, and steady precession follows at right angles, with nutation as the short-lived side branch.

examples.question: A gyro rotor has moment of inertia I = 0.02 kg·m² and spins at 24,000 rpm. A steady torque T = 0.01 N·m is applied. Find the angular momentum H and the precession rate Ω in degrees per minute. Compare Ω with Earth's rate of 15.04 °/h.
steps: Convert spin rate to rad/s: ω = 24,000 × 2π ÷ 60 = 2513.27 rad/s.
Precession rate in rad/s: Ω = T/H = 0.01 ÷ 50.265 = 1.9894 × 10⁻⁴ rad/s.
Convert to degrees per second: 1.9894 × 10⁻⁴ × 180 ÷ π = 0.011399 °/s.
Earth rate in degrees per minute: 15.04 ÷ 60 = 0.2507 °/min. The ratio is 0.6839 ÷ 0.2507 = 2.73.
examples.answer: H = 50.265 kg·m²/s and Ω = 0.684 °/min, about 2.73 times Earth's 0.251 °/min.
examples.check:
import math
omega = 24000 * 2 * math.pi / 60
H = 0.02 * omega
Omega = 0.01 / H
deg_min = Omega * 180 / math.pi * 60
earth = 15.04 / 60
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(H, 3))
print(round(Omega, 8))
print(round(deg_min, 4))
print(round(earth, 4))

traps: Drawing precession along the push. The spin axis moves at right angles to the torque, in the direction that carries H toward T.
Treating nutation as the steady motion. Nutation is a short transient after a sudden torque; damping removes it, leaving steady precession.
Putting rpm directly into Ω = T/(Iω). Convert to rad/s first; otherwise Ω comes out too small by a factor of 2π/60.
Mixing real drift with apparent drift. Bearing friction and imbalance are real; Earth rate and transport rate are apparent and depend on latitude and heading.
Calling a turn coordinator an attitude indicator. It is a rate gyro: it shows rate of turn and roll, not a steady bank angle.

quiz.q: Define rigidity in space for a gyroscope.
quiz.a: With no external torque, the spin axis keeps a fixed direction in inertial space; the rotor's angular momentum H = Iω stays constant.

quiz.q: Why does the spin axis precess at right angles to the applied torque instead of moving along the push?
quiz.a: Torque changes angular momentum: dH points along T. The tip of H moves toward T, so the axis turns at right angles to the torque in the sense of the spin.

quiz.q: A rotor has I = 0.05 kg·m² and spins at 12,000 rpm. A steady torque of 0.02 N·m acts. Find Ω in degrees per minute.
Why must a heading indicator be reset to the magnetic compass during flight?
quiz.a: It is a directional gyro with real drift from friction and imbalance, and apparent drift from Earth rate and transport rate. It holds a direction but does not sense north, so the pilot resets it periodically to the magnetic compass.
A short wobble of the spin axis after a sudden torque, before the axis settles into steady precession; damping removes it.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a rate gyro and a vertical gyro.
quiz.a: A rate gyro measures rate of turn and is used in the turn coordinator; a vertical gyro is erected to the local vertical and measures pitch and roll in the attitude indicator.

quiz.q: At latitude 30°, find the apparent drift of a directional gyro about the local vertical.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ring laser gyros measure the Sagnac phase shift between two light beams travelling opposite ways around a closed cavity. Fibre-optic gyros do the same with light in a coil of fibre, and MEMS gyros use vibrating silicon structures. These sensors feed the inertial navigation systems in 5.5. Search for Sagnac effect, ring laser gyro dither, and MEMS Coriolis gyroscope.
